paras: The lynching threat against Charles Davis took place at Upper Marlboro, Maryland, in August 1915, when talk of lynching Davis, a Black man held in the county jail on horse-stealing charges, led Sheriff Hardy to post an armed guard. No attack on the jail was reported, and the guard was withdrawn the next day.

Davis, described by the Evening Star as "colored" and a resident of Washington, was jailed at Upper Marlboro after Sheriff Hardy investigated the disappearance of two horses in May. He was accused of taking a horse from Benjamin Bowie, later sold for $10 and recovered, and one from Bruce Buck, which was reportedly worked and starved until a policeman in Washington killed it. Davis denied the charge but, according to the Star, admitted he had possessed one of the horses and said he had bought it from "John Brown of Richmond."
The local Prince George's Enquirer gave a different account of his arrest, saying he walked into town on a Monday evening, was recognized, and lived as a huckster near Tenleytown.

According to the Washington Times, the indignation against Davis arose on Wednesday night and stemmed from his alleged treatment of Buck's horse rather than the theft itself. On the night of August 12, after Sheriff Hardy heard a report that a lynching had been discussed, guards were placed at the jail. Accounts of the guard varied: the Star counted two guards inside the jail, the Times described an armed guard surrounding it, and the Alexandria Gazette reported "a squad of special deputies, armed with rifles."

On August 13 the sheriff withdrew the guard, telling the Times that "there was no demonstration against Davis" and that the guard had been placed "to be on the safe side." Davis was to be arraigned for a preliminary hearing before Justice of the Peace J. Alfred Ridgley the following Tuesday, with witnesses expected from Washington. The coverage does not show the result of the hearing or any trial.

The episode was covered by Washington-area papers drawing on the sheriff's statements. The Times attributed the talk to "a group under the influence of liquor," while the Star said it was started by a man "who probably had been imbibing too freely." Both papers gave as much space to the horse's starvation as to the threat, and the Star headlined its story "Guards Against Lynching."

The Prince George's Enquirer, the county weekly, did not mention the lynching talk, expressed sympathy for Buck, and hoped that if Davis was guilty he would be "convicted and punished severely." The Alexandria Gazette printed a one-sentence brief, twice on the same page, which broke off at Davis's name. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

The papers differ on when Davis was arrested: the Enquirer said Monday evening, while the Star's correspondent wrote that he was lodged in jail on the night of August 11, the day he returned to the county. They also differ on his home, given as Washington by the Star and the Times and as Montgomery County near Tenleytown by the Enquirer.

reader.title: Lynching threat against Charles Davis
bases: Lynching talk against a jailed Black prisoner led the sheriff to post an armed guard; no attempt on the jail was reported (A2, A3, A5).

No one was killed; the papers report only talk of lynching, by one man (A3) or a drinking group (A2), and the sheriff said there was 'no demonstration' (A2). The talk was framed as punishment for the alleged theft and starving of a horse (A2, A3).

The Evening Star and the Washington Times both report lynching talk and a guard posted at the jail (A2, A3), and the Alexandria Gazette brief agrees on the guard and the threats (A5), though all rest largely on the sheriff's account.

accounts.label: Sheriff Hardy (Washington Times)
accounts.gist: The guard was a precaution after a report that violence might be attempted; the talk came from a group under the influence of liquor, and there was no general movement to break into the jail.

accounts.label: Sheriff Hardy (Evening Star)
accounts.gist: The talk was started by a man who had probably been drinking; Hardy did not believe there was danger but put two guards in the jail.

accounts.label: Wire brief
accounts.gist: Special deputies armed with rifles guarded the jail where a Black man threatened with lynching was held.

framing.detail: The Washington Times headlined 'Withdraw Guards at Marlboro Jail' and the Evening Star 'Guards Against Lynching', both centering the sheriff's precautions and the alleged mistreatment of the horse.
The local Prince George's Enquirer omitted the lynching talk and hoped Davis, if guilty, would be 'convicted and punished severely'.
The Alexandria Gazette ran a one-sentence brief on the armed deputies among other news items.
